:::{#thm-diff-implies-cont}
#### Differentiability implies continuity

If $f$ is differentiable at $x = c$, then $f$ is continuous at $x = c$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Theorem 2.1, p. 106]

:::

::: proof
Because $f'(c)$ exists, $f(c)$ is defined, and:

$$
\ba
\lim_{h \to 0} \paren{f(c + h) - f(c)}
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \paren{\frac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h} \cd h}
&& \text{(multiply and divide by } h \neq 0 \text{)}
\\
&= \paren{\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h}} \cd \paren{\lim_{h \to 0} h}
&& \text{(limit of a product, both limits exist)}
\\
&= f'(c) \cd 0
&& \text{(definition of } f'(c) \text{)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(multiply)}
\ea
$$

So $\lim_{h \to 0} f(c + h) = f(c)$,
which is $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ with $x = c + h$;
all three conditions of @def-continuous hold.
:::
